title: NVLink prefetch window thrashing: case study and repro notes
body:
Summary:

Short: observed periodic latency spikes (~2–3x token latency) on multi-GPU p2 inference pools when request mix contains a small fraction (~5%) long-context decoders. Nsight traces show repeated NVLink peer-to-peer memcpy bursts aligned with kernel launches, interleaved with short idle gaps. Hypothesis: prefetch window sizing + NVLink transfer scheduling is causing kernel launch backpressure and SM thrashing (lots of short kernels interleaved with transfers).

Why this matters:
- Causes tail latency regressions for bursty workloads (PLG routes with mixed lengths).
- Hard to reproduce in microbench because it depends on request interleaving and cross-GPU KV cache prefetch behavior.
- Existing mitigations (larger microbatching, delaying prefetch) reduce throughput or increase cold latency.

What we did (high-level experiment):
1) Reproduced on a 4xA100 NVLink-connected box (internal lab). Serving runtime pinned to a single host process, 4 devices, persistent model shards.
2) Created synthetic workload: 95% short sequences (32 tokens), 5% long decode sequences (1024 tokens) arriving with Poisson arrivals (mean rps tuned).
3) Traced with Nsight Systems (samples + timeline, 1s captures centered on a spike). Also enabled CUPTI kernel timestamps and NVTX markers in runtime.
4) Captured PCIe and NVLink transfer events and overlaid with kernel launches, memcpy streams, and GPU-side occupancy.

Repro steps (quick):
- Start runtime: ./bin/serving-runtime --model model-v2 --persistent-shards --kv-prefetch=on --prefetch-window=64 --batcher-config=default
- Load harness: python tools/mixed_length_replay.py --clients 120 --short-len 32 --long-len 1024 --long-percent 5 --seed 42
- Nsight capture (host): nv-nsight-cu-cli --sample true --target-processes all --capture-range ctrace --output spike-capture.ncu-rep --duration 1s --process-name serving-runtime
- Also collect nvidia-smi dmon (1s) and nvlink stats (nvidia-smi nvlink --status) for the duration.

Key Nsight observations (from sampled timelines):
- Pattern: 3–5 short kernels (decoding and softmax) launched on GPU0, immediately followed by a sequence of nvlink memcpy events moving prefetched KV pages from GPU1->GPU0. The memcpy window is bursty (large transfers ~MBs) and occupies the NVLink for ~10–30ms depending on prefetch-window size.
- During NVLink bursts, kernel launches on GPU0 are still scheduled but observe long enqueue-to-start gaps (kernel queuing backlog) and SM occupancy drops (SMs idle while host-side enqueue is blocked waiting for DMA-complete sync points).
- When multiple GPUs try to prefetch concurrently (worst when two long requests overlap), NVLink arbitration causes visible tailing: transfers interleave and kernels on both GPUs get fragmented, increasing serialization overhead and per-token latency.
- CUDA graph captures show fragmented graph replay where memcpy ops appear between graph kernels due to runtime-inserted prefetch barriers.

Microbench variations tried:
- Prefetch window sizes: 16, 32, 64, 128, 256 pages. Smaller windows reduce NVLink bursts but increase number of prefetch ops and overhead; larger windows cause bigger contiguous transfers that dominate NVLink for longer.
- Prefetch scheduling: immediate (current), staggered (introduce 2–5ms offset between devices), and host-serialized (single device prefetch at a time). Staggering significantly reduced simultaneous NVLink bursts and lowered tail latency without hurting throughput much in lab tests.
- Async memcpy stream placement: moving prefetch memcpy to a dedicated high-priority stream (stream priority > kernels) reduced enqueue blocking but starved kernels sometimes; reversed priorities removed starvation but reintroduced queueing delays.
- Waveform profiling: SM occupancy heatmaps show cyclic drop-offs correlated with NVLink saturation windows.

Quantitative numbers (single run representative):
- Baseline (prefetch-window=64, immediate): p95 token latency = 180ms, p99 = 280ms (spikes visible).
- Staggered prefetch (2ms offsets across GPUs): p95 = 140ms, p99 = 165ms.
- No prefetch (lazy fetch on demand): p95 = 160ms, p99 = 190ms, but cold-step latency for first tokens of long requests increased by ~80ms.
- Larger prefetch-window=256: p95 = 220ms, p99 = 410ms (bad).

Interpreting the data / hypotheses refined:
- NVLink behaves like a shared narrow pipe: large burst transfers from multiple GPUs contend and produce serialization. Smaller, more frequent transfers reduce per-transfer time but increase CPU/host overhead and transfer counts.
- The runtime currently uses coarse-grained prefetch semantics (grab N pages eagerly per request). When two sockets (gpus) do this concurrently we get synchronized bursts.
- Kernel launch enqueue appears blocked in some windows because cudaStreamSynchronize or event waits are being used to guarantee KV coherence before decoding proceeds; those wait points starve SMs while NVLink copy completes.

Short-term mitigations (practical):
- Enable staggered prefetch by default in multi-GPU host: add small jitter offsets based on GPU index. Cheap, reduces simultaneous NVLink saturation.
- Reduce default prefetch-window to 32 for NVLink-connected multi-GPU hosts; allow workload-driven override.
- Implement backoff: if nvlink bandwidth counters exceed threshold, slow down prefetch rate for subsequent requests (adaptive). Requires low-overhead NVLink telemetry (nvsmi) sampling or extrapolation from dmon.

Longer-term changes to explore:
- Prefetch coalescing at runtime: aggregate small prefetches across concurrent requests into a single scheduled window with controlled NVLink timing.
- Move to a peer-to-peer pull model where the serving GPU pulls pages in small pieces as kernels request KV, decoupling from host-enforced prefetch barriers.
- Use RDMA-like coordination between GPUs to orchestrate transfer windows (complicated).

Open questions / TODOs:
- How representative is this on cloud infra vs our lab NVLink topology? Need captures from Dedicated clusters (JIRA-REND-319).
- Does NVSwitch (DGX style) behave differently? Schedule a run on nv-switch machines (infra ticket INFRA-612).
- Can we instrument NVLink instantaneous bandwidth cheaply in prod? nvidia-smi nvlink sampling is heavy; consider aggregate heuristics from per-device PCIe counters.
- Verify interplay with CUDA graphs: are graphs inserting copies due to prefetch APIs we call? (Check PR #1487 where graph replay logic changed).

Files attached / artifacts:
- spike-capture.ncu-rep (nsight capture) -- stored in GDrive folder under traces/spike-capture-2026-01-08.ncu-rep
- dmon logs: dmon-spike-2026-01-08.csv
- short python harness: tools/mixed_length_replay.py (branch: perf/nvlink-prefetch)

Notes to self / meeting bullets:
- Try staggered prefetch in canary Dedicated pool next week. If p99 improves, roll to default.
- Add lightweight nvlink usage counters to runtime debug endpoint to allow telemetry without heavy nsight captures.
- Raise infra request for NVSwitch runs and report back by 2026-01-20.

References:
- Related ticket: JIRA-REND-319 (NVLink prefetch tail latencies)
- PR that touched graph replay and prefetch points: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1487
- Confluence note: CONFLUENCE-8742 (prefetch design doc)

Unresolved intuition: is the kernel queuing gap due to host CPU scheduling (we saw kworker spikes) or purely due to device-side NVLink arbitration? Need combined host kernel timelines + nsight to disambiguate.

End (Ava)

-- edit 2026-01-12: added p95/p99 numbers from repeat run and updated suggested default prefetch-window to 32 for NVLink hosts.
